title: Lifestyles

summary: Students learn words for the body, injuries and food, use the zero and first conditional and a few / a little, build word families, and practice asking for help.

grammar.title: Zero and First Conditional
grammar.rule: Use the zero conditional for things that are always true: If + present, present. Use the first conditional for a possible result in the future: If + present, will / won't + verb. When the “if” part comes first, put a comma after it.
grammar.form: Zero: If + simple present, simple present | First: If + simple present, will / won't + verb
examples: If you heat ice, it melts.
We feel better if we rest well.
If you fall over, I'll help you.
If it rains tomorrow, we won't go to the park.

items.prompt: If you touch fire, it ___ your hand.
items.explanation: This is always true, so we use the zero conditional: If + present, present.

items.prompt: If Omar eats too much pizza tonight, he ___ feel sick.
items.explanation: This is a possible future result, so we use will + verb.

items.prompt: If it ___ tomorrow, we will stay at home.
items.explanation: After “if” we use the simple present, even when we talk about the future.

items.prompt: Plants die if they ___ get water.
items.explanation: This is a fact (zero conditional), so both parts use the simple present.

items.prompt: Which sentence is a zero conditional?
options: If you mix red and blue, you get purple.
If you come, I'll make tea.
If she studies, she will pass.
items.answer: If you mix red and blue, you get purple.
items.explanation: The zero conditional uses the present in both parts for something always true.

items.prompt: If you ___ your hands with soap, they get clean.
items.explanation: Zero conditional: If + simple present (wash), simple present (get).

items.prompt: If you heat water to 100 degrees, it ___.
items.explanation: A scientific fact uses the zero conditional: it boils.

items.prompt: If Sara ___ to the pharmacy, she will buy some medicine.
items.explanation: After “if” we use the simple present: Sara goes.

items.prompt: If you study tonight, you ___ the test tomorrow.
answer: will pass
'll pass
items.explanation: “Tomorrow” is a future result, so we use will + verb.

items.prompt: If it ___, we will play football after school.
answer: does not rain
doesn't rain
items.explanation: After “if” use the simple present. Negative with it: doesn't + verb.

items.prompt: If you eat too many sweets, you ___ a toothache.
answer: get
will get
'll get
items.explanation: This is generally true, so “get” (zero) or “will get” (first) both work.

items.prompt: If I finish my homework, I ___ you later.
answer: will call
'll call
items.explanation: “Later” is the future, so the result uses will + verb.

items.answer: I will help you if you fall over.
alt: If you fall over I will help you.
items.explanation: First conditional: will + verb in the result, simple present after if.

items.answer: Ice melts if it gets warm.
alt: If it gets warm ice melts.
items.explanation: Zero conditional: simple present in both parts.

items.answer: Will you come if I invite you?
alt: If I invite you will you come?
items.explanation: Question: Will + subject + verb, then if + simple present.

items.answer: She won't feel sick if she rests.
alt: If she rests she won't feel sick.
items.explanation: won't + verb in the result, simple present after if.

items.prompt: Fahad studies. He will pass the test.
answer: If Fahad studies, he will pass the test.
If Fahad studies, he'll pass the test.
If Fahad studies he will pass the test.
If Fahad studies he'll pass the test.
items.explanation: If + simple present, will + verb. Use a comma after the if part.

items.instruction: Change the result to the negative (won't).
items.prompt: If it rains, we will play outside.
answer: If it rains, we won't play outside.
If it rains, we will not play outside.
If it rains we won't play outside.
If it rains we will not play outside.
items.explanation: will → won't (will not). Rain means no playing outside!

items.prompt: You get wet if you walk in the rain.
answer: If you walk in the rain, you get wet.
If you walk in the rain you get wet.
items.explanation: Move the if part to the front and add a comma.

items.prompt: If I go to the pharmacy, you will come with me.
answer: If I go to the pharmacy, will you come with me?
If I go to the pharmacy will you come with me?
Will you come with me if I go to the pharmacy?
items.explanation: Move will before you: will you come ...?

items.sentence: If it will rain tomorrow, we will stay home.
items.answer: If it rains tomorrow, we will stay home.
items.explanation: Don't use will after “if”. Use the simple present: If it rains.

items.sentence: If you mix yellow and blue, you get green.
items.answer: If you mix yellow and blue, you get green.
items.explanation: Correct! A fact, so the zero conditional is right.

items.sentence: If she eat too much, she will feel sick.
items.answer: If she eats too much, she will feel sick.
items.explanation: With she, the simple present verb needs -s: eats.

items.sentence: If I see Reem, I tell her tomorrow.
items.answer: If I see Reem, I will tell her tomorrow.
items.explanation: “Tomorrow” is the future, so the result needs will + verb.

items.sentence: We'll go to the beach if the weather is nice.
items.answer: We'll go to the beach if the weather is nice.
items.explanation: Correct! will + verb in the result, simple present after if.

grammar.title: a few / a little
grammar.rule: Use “a few” with countable nouns, things you can count (eggs, strawberries, spoons). Use “a little” with uncountable nouns, things you can't count (salt, milk, bread, jam). Both mean “some, but not a lot”.
grammar.form: a few + plural countable noun | a little + uncountable noun
examples: Add a few strawberries and a little milk.
There are a few olives on the plate.
I'd like a little salt, please.
We need a few eggs for the cake.

items.prompt: Can I have ___ milk, please?
items.explanation: We can't count milk, so we use a little.

items.prompt: There are ___ eggs in the fridge.
items.explanation: We can count eggs, so we use a few.

items.prompt: Put ___ salt on the eggs.
items.explanation: Salt is uncountable, so we use a little.

items.prompt: I ate ___ strawberries after lunch.
items.explanation: Strawberries are countable (one strawberry, two strawberries), so we use a few.

items.prompt: Which word can go after “a little”?
items.explanation: Jam is uncountable, so we say a little jam.

items.prompt: Which word can go after “a few”?
items.explanation: Forks are countable and plural, so we say a few forks.

items.prompt: We need ___ olives for the salad.
items.explanation: Olives are countable, so we use a few.

items.prompt: Add ___ pepper to the soup.
items.explanation: Pepper (the powder) is uncountable, so we use a little.

items.prompt: I put ___ jam on my bread.
items.explanation: Jam is uncountable, so we use a little.

items.prompt: There are ___ spoons on the table.
items.explanation: Spoons are countable, so we use a few.

items.prompt: My brother drinks ___ milk with his cereal.
items.explanation: Milk is uncountable, so we use a little.

items.prompt: She ate a few ___.
items.explanation: After “a few” we need a plural countable noun: strawberries.

items.prompt: Can I have a little ___, please?
items.explanation: After “a little” we need an uncountable noun: bread.

items.answer: Add a little salt to the eggs.
items.explanation: a little + uncountable noun (salt).

items.answer: There are a few strawberries left.
items.explanation: a few + plural countable noun (strawberries).

items.answer: Can I have a little jam?
items.explanation: a little + uncountable noun (jam).

items.answer: We need a few forks and spoons.
alt: We need a few spoons and forks.
items.explanation: a few + plural countable nouns (forks and spoons).

items.prompt: There is some milk in the glass.
answer: There is a little milk in the glass.
There's a little milk in the glass.
items.explanation: Milk is uncountable: a little milk.

items.prompt: I have some olives.
answer: I have a few olives.
items.explanation: Olives are countable: a few olives.

items.prompt: Put some pepper on it.
answer: Put a little pepper on it.
items.explanation: Pepper is uncountable: a little pepper.

items.prompt: She made some pizzas for the party.
answer: She made a few pizzas for the party.
items.explanation: “Pizzas” is plural and countable: a few pizzas.

items.sentence: Can I have a few bread?
items.answer: Can I have a little bread?
items.explanation: Bread is uncountable, so we use a little.
Eggs are countable, so we use a few.

items.sentence: Add a little salt and a few strawberries.
items.answer: Add a little salt and a few strawberries.
items.explanation: Correct! a little + salt (uncountable), a few + strawberries (countable).
Milk is uncountable, so we use a little.

reading.title: Breakfast for Mom
reading.text:
Mom was not feeling well, so Fahad and his sister Reem decided to make her a healthy breakfast.

“If we make breakfast, Mom will have a rest,” said Reem. Fahad agreed. They boiled a few eggs. Then Reem took out the bread, a little jam and a few strawberries.

Fahad wanted to cut the strawberries with a big, sharp knife. “Be careful!” said Reem. But it was too late. “Ouch! I cut my finger!” Fahad cried.

At first, Fahad didn't want to tell anyone. He felt silly. Then he remembered his teacher's words: “If you need help, ask for it. Everyone needs help sometimes.” So he went to find his father.

Dad washed the cut with soap and water and put a bandage on it. “Next time, ask me before you use the big knife,” he said kindly. “If you ask, I will always help you.”

Finally, they carried the breakfast to Mom: boiled eggs, bread with jam, strawberries and a glass of warm milk. Mom smiled. “Thank you both. This is the best medicine!” she said.

reading.title: My Food Adventures
reading.text:
Hi, I'm Sara! I love trying new food, and this blog is about my food adventures.

Last winter, my family went to AlJouf. AlJouf is famous for its olives. We visited an olive farm, and the farmer gave us a few green olives to try. They were salty and a little bitter! If you go to AlJouf, you will see olive trees everywhere.

In the summer, we went to Jeddah. We ate fresh fish at a restaurant near the sea. The cook put a little salt and pepper on the fish, and it was delicious.

My favorite food adventure was at home. My aunt showed me how to make pizza. We used a little cheese, a few tomatoes and a few olives from AlJouf. If you bake pizza for too long, it burns, so we watched it carefully!

Here is my top tip: when you try a new food, take a small bite first. If you don't like it, that's OK. If you like it, you will have a new favorite food!

reading.title: Khalid's Big Fall
reading.text:
On Sunday afternoon, Khalid and his friends were playing football in the school yard. Khalid was running fast with the ball when he fell over. “Ouch! My knee!” he shouted.

His knee was red and sore, and there was a small cut on his elbow. Coach Majed ran over. “Can you move your toes?” he asked. Khalid moved them. “Good,” said the coach. “I don't think anything is broken.”

The coach washed the cut with soap and a little water. Then he put a bandage on Khalid's elbow. “If you play on that knee today, it will get worse,” he said. “Sit down and rest.”

After school, Khalid's mother took him to the pharmacy. The pharmacist gave them a little medicine for the pain. “If you put ice on a sore knee, it feels better,” she said. “Do it a few times a day.”

Khalid was sad because there was a big match on Thursday. But he rested and put ice on his knee every evening. After a few days, his knee didn't hurt anymore.

On Thursday, Khalid played in the match, and he scored the winning goal! “If I get hurt again, I will rest first,” he thought.

reading.title: Stay Safe in the Kitchen
reading.text:
Cooking is fun, but the kitchen can be a dangerous place. Here are some simple rules to keep you safe.

Wash your hands first. If you touch food with dirty hands, germs get into the food. So always wash your hands with soap and warm water before you start.

Be careful with knives. A sharp knife can cut your finger very easily. Always cut away from your hand, and ask an adult to help you. Young children can use a butter knife to spread jam on their bread.

Watch out for hot things. If you touch a hot pan, you burn your hand. If you get a small burn, put it under cool water for ten minutes. Don't put butter or ice on it! For a big burn, get help from an adult quickly.

Clean up spills. If milk falls on the floor, someone might slip and fall over. Clean it up right away with a few paper towels.

Use the right tools. If you need a little salt or sugar, use a spoon, not your fingers!

Remember: if you follow these rules, you will have a safe and happy time in the kitchen.

reading.title: My Healthy Breakfast Plan
reading.text:
Dear Grandma,

How are you? I hope your sore throat is better now. Mom told me you went to the pharmacy for some medicine last week.

I have exciting news! Next week is Healthy Food Week at my school. Every class is going to make a healthy breakfast table, and my class chose me to plan the menu. Here is my plan.

First, we will have cereal with a little milk and a few strawberries on top. Strawberries make the cereal sweet, so we don't need sugar.

Next, there will be boiled eggs with a little salt and pepper. Our teacher says that if you eat eggs in the morning, you feel full for a long time.

We will also have brown bread with a little olive oil and a few black olives. That's your favorite breakfast, Grandma!

Some girls in my class wanted pizza, but I said no. Pizza is delicious, but it isn't a healthy breakfast. If we win the competition, our class will get a special prize.

Can you send me your recipe for date jam? If you send it, I will make some for our table.

Love,
Nouf

wordWork.title: Word families
wordWork.rule: A word family is a group of words made from the same base word, like help, helper, helpful and helping. Endings such as -er, -ful, -y, -ion and -ing change the job of the word in a sentence.

items.prompt: Thank you for carrying my bag! You are very ___.
items.explanation: help + -ful makes the adjective helpful.

items.prompt: My ___ explained the lesson again.
items.explanation: teach + -er makes the person who teaches: teacher.

items.prompt: Which word is in the same family as “create”?
items.explanation: create → creation. Cream and crate are different words.

items.prompt: Vegetables and fruit are ___ food.
items.explanation: health + -y makes the adjective healthy.

items.prompt: Be ___ with that knife! It's sharp.
items.explanation: care + -ful makes the adjective careful.

items.prompt: Which word is NOT in the “help” family?
items.explanation: Helpful and helper come from help. Hello is a different word.

items.prompt: Oh no! My arm is ___.
items.explanation: break → broken. We use broken as an adjective.

items.prompt: Omar is a very fast ___.
items.explanation: swim → swimmer: double the m and add -er for the person who swims.

items.prompt: What do you call a person who bakes bread?
items.explanation: bake + -r makes the person: baker. A bakery is the shop.
